extracted.intended_audience: aspiring writers, dramatists, and literary critics (general reading public)
extracted.subtask_description: Practical and critical advice for writers and theatre critics about style, metaphor, pleasing an audience, and the proper temper of criticism, drawn from Spectator essays. Emphasises clarity, tasteful use of rules, and avoiding common stylistic faults.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treat love agreeably to please broad audiences
rubrics_metrics.description: 'a Subject which when agreeably handled, can scarce fail of being well receiv'd by both Sexes.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If writing on love, handle the subject agreeably — well-treated love subjects are likely to please both men and women. Use light, agreeable treatment; illustrative maxims and sonnets can succeed. (Example: the included maxims and a sonnet are presented as effective, above-ordinary examples.)

rubrics_metrics.name: First precept in poetry: to please
rubrics_metrics.description: The author asserts that 'the first Precept in Poetry were not to please' (used to justify that pleasing the audience is a primary aim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not dismiss popular success as inherently disqualifying; pleasing the audience is a legitimate and central aim of poetry and drama. Critics should recognise that long runs or popularity may reflect an important aesthetic quality (the capacity to please).

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not condemn works merely because they are popular
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics should not 'fall upon a Play, not because it is ill written, but because it takes' or assume 'whatever Dramatick Performance has a long Run, must of Necessity be good for nothing.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid the anti-popularity bias: judging a play harshly solely because it has a long run (or is popular) is an improper critical posture. Evaluate on merits, not on resentment of success.

rubrics_metrics.name: True critic: learned, generous, and able to discover beauties
rubrics_metrics.description: A 'true Critick' is likened to Aristotle, Longinus, Horace, Quintilian, Boileau — learned critics who 'discover Beauties which escaped the Observation of the Vulgar, and very often find out Reasons for palliating and excusing such little Slips and Oversights.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good criticism requires learning (knowledge of classical authors and languages), the ability to perceive subtle beauties, and a charitable disposition to explain or palliate small faults. Contrast with smatterers who depreciate and cavil at celebrated works.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid unintelligible jargon and pretentious authority
rubrics_metrics.description: Words like 'Unity, Action, Sentiment, and Diction, pronounced with an Air of Authority, give them a Figure among unlearned Readers' — many critics are unintelligible and use jargon to impress.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not rely on obscure technical terms or air of authority to persuade; clarity matters. Criticism should be intelligible and grounded in understanding, not in unintelligible pronouncements that fool the unlearned.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recognise that deviation from rules can be good judgment
rubrics_metrics.description: 'There is sometimes a greater Judgment shewn in deviating from the Rules of Art, than in adhering to them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rules of art are guides, not absolute laws. Writers and dramatists may intentionally depart from established rules when such deviation produces a higher beauty or the sublime (the 'Gusto Grande'). Critics should judge such departures by their resulting effect, not only by conformity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Great genius may surpass rule-following craft
rubrics_metrics.description: There is 'more Beauty in the Works of a great Genius who is ignorant of all the Rules of Art, than in the Works of a little Genius, who not only knows, but scrupulously observes them.' (Shakespeare cited as example.)
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate work for its overall artistic power and originality; technical correctness is not the sole measure. Exceptional originality or force can justify irregularities; prefer powerful invention to sterile correctness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of metaphor
rubrics_metrics.description: A metaphor is 'a Simile in one Word, which serves to convey the Thoughts of the Mind under Resemblances and Images which affect the Senses.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use metaphors to create vivid sensory resemblances. Understand the function of metaphor before employing it: it should create an apt image that appeals to the senses and clarifies thought.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid mixing inconsistent metaphors
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'Mixture of inconsistent Metaphors' is a frequent fault: combining heterogeneous images produces 'Confusion, Obscurity, and Noise.' Example: a hero compared simultaneously to a Thunderbolt, a Lion, and the Sea leading to absurd blended images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure metaphors are homogeneous and consistent; do not fuse images from incompatible domains. Test metaphor combinations by imagining them painted — if the resulting picture is absurd or impossible, the metaphor mix is wrong.

rubrics_metrics.name: Keep metaphorical images sensorially consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: An image taken from what acts upon the Sight 'cannot, without Violence, be applied to the Hearing; and so of the rest.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Match the sense-domain of your image to its target: don't apply visual imagery to auditory phenomena, etc. This preserves clarity and prevents strained or violent comparisons.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not give metaphors impossible agency
rubrics_metrics.description: It is an impropriety 'to make any Being in Nature or Art to do things in its Metaphorical State, which it could not do in its Original.' Example: 'the heavy Lashes that have dropped from your Pen' mixes incompatible actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid constructions that require a metaphorical entity to perform actions impossible for the literal referent; such usage produces nonsense. Check whether the actions implied by the metaphor make sense for the literal object.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid running metaphors into tedious allegory or digression
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'running of Metaphors into tedious Allegories' leads writers to wander from their subject 'for a Page together' — e.g., taking 'a World of Charms' and elaborating poles and zones at length.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep similes and metaphors concise and on-topic. Do not let the allure of one image lead to a prolonged allegorical excursion that distracts from the subject; maintain focus and economy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Write as you think to be intelligible
rubrics_metrics.description: 'If ordinary Authors would condescend to write as they think, they would at least be allow'd the Praise of being intelligible.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritise natural, straightforward expression over ostentatious ornamentation. Clarity and directness in expressing one's thoughts will earn the basic praise of intelligibility; affected style often masks weak sense.

rubrics_metrics.name: Beware of malicious or ignorant criticism (motivation of critics)
rubrics_metrics.description: Envy and cavil are 'the natural Fruits of Laziness and Ignorance' — many critics 'vilifie and depreciate every new Production that gains Applause' out of ill-will or inability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating criticism, account for critics' motives: detracting reviews may stem from laziness, ignorance, or envy rather than sound aesthetic judgment. A fair critic should avoid personal malice and ground critique in reasoned observation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical vocabulary for drama: Unity, Action, Sentiment, Diction
rubrics_metrics.description: The text highlights the words 'Unity, Action, Sentiment, and Diction' as common critical touchstones (often pronounced with authority by uninformed critics).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These focal terms represent legitimate dimensions for dramatic evaluation (structure, plot movement, emotional content, and language). Use them precisely and intelligibly rather than as rhetorical badges of authority.
